In this blog I'll run through how I drew plasmid maps in R using the plasmapR package https://bradyajohnston.github.io/plasmapR/ (written by Brady Johnston). I found the default map too busy, and I wanted control over which genes were labelled and the colours used, so I modified the ggplot object that plasmapR returns. I'll be drawing a map for a single plasmid. You can download the plasmid sequence [here](https://github.com/sburgess2/blogs/tree/main/2026/2026-10-10-plasmidmap/data).

The plasmid sequence originates from an *Escherichia coli* strain isolated from dairy cattle faeces. The plasmid was assembled using Flye and annotated using Prokka as described in [Burgess et al (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.idairyj.2021.104998).

## Packages

plasmapR isn't on CRAN, so it needs to be installed from GitHub.

```{r}
#| eval: false

devtools::install_github("bradyajohnston/plasmapr")
```

First load the libraries we'll be using.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(plasmapR)
```

### Reading in the data

Next read the GenBank file into the plasmid object with `read_gb()`.

```{r}
fl <- "2026/2026-10-10-plasmidmap/data/pEE072d2.gb"
plasmid <- fl |> read_gb()
```

Then we can convert the plasmid object into a data frame using `as.data.frame()`.

```{r}
df <- plasmid |>
  as.data.frame()
```

Here are the first six rows of this data frame:

```{r}
head(df)
```

### Grouping the genes by predicted function

This data frame contains three types of sequences. The source:

```{r}
df |> filter(type == "source")
```

The miscellaneous features:

```{r}
df |> filter(type == "misc_feature")
```

The coding sequences (CDS), showing the first ten rows:

```{r}
df |>
  filter(type == "CDS") |>
  head(10)
```

Many of the miscellaneous features overlap a CDS, which pushes the arrows off the ring, so I kept only the CDS.

```{r}
#| eval: false

df |>
  filter(type == "CDS")
```

Next, we'll use `mutate()` and `case_when()` to add a column called `annotation`, which will group each gene by its predicted function (Mobilisation, ESBL, Plasmid replication and partitioning, Plasmid transfer, and Other), based on the gene name. `case_when()` works through the conditions in order and stops at the first match, so the order matters. The `str_detect()` function is used to look for a pattern (in this case certain gene names) in a string (in this case the `name` column). Anything not matched, including the hypothetical proteins (e.g. EE0072d_05113), ends up as "Other".

```{r}
#| eval: false

df |>
  mutate(
    annotation = case_when(
      str_detect(name, "IS903") ~ "Mobilisation",
      str_detect(name, "^bla") ~ "ESBL",
      str_detect(
        name,
        "^Ori$|^rep|^par"
      ) ~ "Plasmid replication and partitioning",
      str_detect(name, "^tra|^trb|^finO") ~ "Plasmid transfer",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    name = name |>
      str_replace("bla_1", "blaCTX-M") |>
      str_remove("_\\d{1,2}$") |>
      str_remove(" .*$")
  )
```

The *bla*~CTX-M~ gene is named *bla_1* in the annotation, so in the last lines above I renamed it to *bla*~CTX-M~ for the map label. Prokka also adds a number to the end of repeated gene names (e.g. *traI_1*, *traI_2*), so `str_remove()` drops the underscore and the one or two digits that follow it.

The pattern `"_\\d{1,2}$"` is a regular expression, and it can be read piece by piece:

- `_` matches an underscore.
- `\\d` matches any digit (0 to 9). The backslash is doubled because a single backslash has a special meaning inside an R string.
- `{1,2}` means one to two of the thing before it, so `\\d{1,2}` matches one or two digits.
- `$` means the end of the string, so the match only happens when the underscore and digits are the last thing in the name.

Put together, the pattern only matches an underscore followed by one or two digits at the very end of a name. This means *traI_1* becomes *traI*, but the locus tags (e.g. EE0072d_05113) are left alone, because they have five digits after the underscore.

Some of the miscellaneous features also have long names, such as "traG (Yi 2010) hypothetical protein CDS". To keep just the gene name, the last `str_remove()` uses the pattern `" .*$"`:

- The space at the start matches the first space in the name.
- `.` matches any character.
- `*` means zero or more of the thing before it, so `.*` matches any run of characters.
- `$` means the end of the string.

Together, the pattern matches everything from the first space to the end of the name, so "traG (Yi 2010) hypothetical protein CDS" becomes *traG*.

Next, we need to select the columns `plot_plasmid()` expects:

```{r}
#| eval: false

df |>
  select(index, name, type = annotation, start, end, direction)
```

We also need to add a `mid` column (the midpoint of each gene), which is used later to position the gene labels.

```{r}
#| eval: false

df |>
  mutate(mid = (start + end) / 2)
```

We can then chain the code above together and save it into a new object, `df1`.

```{r}
df1 <- df |>
  filter(type == "CDS") |>
  mutate(
    annotation = case_when(
      str_detect(name, "IS903") ~ "Mobilisation",
      str_detect(name, "^bla") ~ "ESBL",
      str_detect(
        name,
        "^Ori$|^rep|^par"
      ) ~ "Plasmid replication and partitioning",
      str_detect(name, "^tra|^trb|^finO") ~ "Plasmid transfer",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    name = name |>
      str_replace("bla_1", "blaCTX-M") |>
      str_remove("_\\d{1,2}$") |>
      str_remove(" .*$")
  ) |>
  select(index, name, type = annotation, start, end, direction) |>
  mutate(mid = (start + end) / 2)
```

I wanted all the genes to be visible on the map, so I kept the "Other" genes. If you don't want them displayed on the plasmid map, you could filter them out using:

```{r}
#| eval: false

df1 |>
  filter_out(type == "Other")
```


### The layers of a plasmid plot

`plot_plasmid()` returns a ggplot object. Here's the default map.

```{r}
pl1 <- df1 |> plot_plasmid()
pl1
```

The default map labels every gene, which gets crowded. After a lot of playing around, I realised that removing some of the layers was the key to getting the map into a format I liked more. The plot is built from layers, which are stored as a list in `pl1$layers`.

```{r}
pl1$layers
```

There are five layers. Layer 1 draws the plasmid backbone (the ring), and layer 3 draws the gene arrows. These are the two layers I kept. Layers 2, 4, and 5 are the `geom_label_repel()` labels, the `geom_fit_text()` text, and the `annotate()` layer. To see what each layer adds, we'll remove them one at a time. 

Removing only layer 1 drops the plasmid backbone, leaving the gene arrows and labels without the ring.

```{r}
pl_no_backbone <- pl1
pl_no_backbone$layers <- pl_no_backbone$layers[-1]
pl_no_backbone
```

Removing only layer 2 drops the `geom_label_repel()` labels, which sit outside the ring with lines pointing to each gene.

```{r}
pl_no_repel <- pl1
pl_no_repel$layers <- pl_no_repel$layers[-2]
pl_no_repel
```

Removing only layer 3 drops the gene arrows, leaving the ring and labels without the genes.

```{r}
pl_no_arrows <- pl1
pl_no_arrows$layers <- pl_no_arrows$layers[-3]
pl_no_arrows
```

Removing only layer 4 drops the `geom_fit_text()` text, which fits some of the gene names inside the arrows (when the arrows are long enough).

```{r}
pl_no_fit_text <- pl1
pl_no_fit_text$layers <- pl_no_fit_text$layers[-4]
pl_no_fit_text
```

Removing only layer 5 drops the `annotate()` layer, which adds text to the centre of the map. If you want to keep the plasmid name and length of your plasmid then keep this layer in.

```{r}
pl_no_annotate <- pl1
pl_no_annotate$layers <- pl_no_annotate$layers[-5]
pl_no_annotate
```

Now that we know what each layer does, we can remove the second, fourth and fifth layer from `pl1`.

```{r}
pl1$layers <- pl1$layers[-c(2, 4, 5)]
```


### Choosing the colours

Where I can, I like to select colours that are relevant to my topic. Given this plasmid contains an antimicrobial resistance gene, I decided to use some of the colours from these two World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week images.

![](images/AMR-Poster.jpg){width="45%"} ![](images/amr-is-invisible-banner-en.jpg){width="50%"}

I uploaded them into <https://imagecolorpicker.com/> to get the hex codes for the two shades of blue and the black from the first image, and the orange from the second image. I used a light grey for the "Other" genes so they're in the background.

We'll use these colours to create a custom palette as follows:

```{r}
custom_colors <- c(
  "Plasmid replication and partitioning" = "#cbe8f6",
  "Plasmid transfer" = "#1898d5",
  "Mobilisation" = "#010103",
  "ESBL" = "#fe6f43",
  "Other" = "#D9D9D9"
)
```

### Building the final plasmid plot

I didn't want the "Other" genes labelled. To do this, we'll add our own `geom_text()` layer that filters out the "Other" genes. Each label sits at the midpoint of its gene and is nudged out from the ring. `append(..., after = 0)` adds the new text layer as the first layer, so it is drawn underneath the gene arrows. Setting `inherit.aes = FALSE` stops the text layer picking up the aesthetics from the plasmapR layers.

```{r}
pl1_modified <- pl1
pl1_modified$layers <- append(
  pl1_modified$layers,
  geom_text(
    data = df1 |>
      filter_out(type == "Other"),
    aes(x = mid, y = 3, label = name),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 3,
    color = "black",
    nudge_y = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ),
  after = 0
)
```

Finally, we'll add the custom colours, remove the background and axes with `theme_void()`, and rename the legend.

```{r}
custom_plot <- pl1_modified +
  scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(fill = "Predicted function")

custom_plot
```

## Drawing maps for multiple plasmids

If you have more than one plasmid, you can wrap the steps above in a function that takes the path to a GenBank file and returns the finished map. Get the map looking right for one plasmid first, then copy the code into the body of the function and replace the file path with the function argument.

```{r}
#| eval: false

make_plasmid_map <- function(fl) {
  df1 <- fl |>
    read_gb() |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    filter(type == "CDS") |>
    mutate(
      annotation = case_when(
        str_detect(name, "IS903") ~ "Mobilisation",
        str_detect(name, "^bla") ~ "ESBL",
        str_detect(
          name,
          "^Ori$|^rep|^par"
        ) ~ "Plasmid replication and partitioning",
        str_detect(name, "^tra|^trb|^finO") ~ "Plasmid transfer",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      name = name |>
        str_replace("bla_1", "blaCTX-M") |>
        str_remove("_\\d{1,2}$") |>
        str_remove(" .*$")
    ) |>
    select(index, name, type = annotation, start, end, direction) |>
    mutate(mid = (start + end) / 2)

  pl <- df1 |> plot_plasmid()
  pl$layers <- pl$layers[-c(2, 4, 5)]
  pl$layers <- append(
    pl$layers,
    geom_text(
      data = df1 |>
        filter_out(type == "Other"),
      aes(x = mid, y = 3, label = name),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      size = 3,
      color = "black",
      nudge_y = 0.5,
      show.legend = FALSE
    ),
    after = 0
  )

  pl +
    scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors) +
    theme_void() +
    labs(fill = "Predicted function")
}
```

You can then use `map()` from purrr to run the function over a vector of file paths, which returns a list of maps.

```{r}
#| eval: false

files <- c(
  "2026/2026-10-10-plasmidmap/data/plasmid_a.gb",
  "2026/2026-10-10-plasmidmap/data/plasmid_b.gb"
)

maps <- files |> map(make_plasmid_map)
```

To put the maps side by side, the patchwork package combines ggplot objects into a single figure. `wrap_plots()` takes a list of plots, and `plot_layout(guides = "collect")` keeps a single shared legend rather than one per map.

```{r}
#| eval: false

library(patchwork)

wrap_plots(maps) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

For two maps, you can also add them together directly with `maps[[1]] + maps[[2]]`.

## Saving the figure

Finally, I saved the map as a PNG sized to a quarter of an A4 page (A6), which is 148 x 105 mm in landscape. The landscape orientation leaves room for the legend beside the map.

```{r}
#| eval: false

ggsave(
  plot = custom_plot,
  filename = "2026/2026-10-10-plasmidmap/output/plasmid_map.png",
  dpi = 1000,
  width = 148,
  height = 105,
  units = "mm"
)
```

## Key tips

- `plot_plasmid()` returns a ggplot object, so you can remove, reorder, or add layers (`pl1$layers`) and change layer parameters directly when the defaults don't quite fit.
- The order of the conditions in `case_when()` matters. Put the most specific groups first.
- Get the map right for one plasmid before wrapping the code in a function. 
- A lot of the work happens before R. Check your annotations (e.g. against the ResFinder output) before you draw the map.
